summary: Defines a new network address format and rules for using some existing network address formats, so that OSI applications can work over non-OSI lower layers. It was on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Different networks write addresses differently. This gives a way to write them so programs can use them anywhere.

questions: how to encode network addresses for non-osi lower layers
what is an osi network address
how to encode ip address in nsap
subtitle: A way to carry TCP/IP and X.25 addressing inside OSI network addresses.

tldr.problem: OSI applications and the OSI Directory identify end systems by OSI Network Addresses, but such applications often run over TCP/IP or X.25 instead of a global OSI Network Service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC encodes the lower-layer information inside a network address: X.121 addresses for international X.25, and a new format using the Telex address type whose decimal domain specific part carries an X.25 DTE or an IP address, port and transport set.
tldr.outcome: The scheme is interim and algorithmic: an OSI application can derive the addressing it needs from the address itself, without a directory service for that step.

today: RFC 1277 is listed as a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes itself as an interim approach for use before a directory service can supply this information.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The OSI Directory stores a Presentation Address that contains OSI Network Addresses. Applications using the Directory must be able to use these to identify end systems. In practice, OSI applications often run over lower layers other than the OSI Network Service, and the RFC says it is neither reasonable nor desirable to depend on a global OSI Network Service.

It therefore defines a new network address format and rules for some existing formats. The scope is any TCP/IP network supporting the OSI Transport Service (COTS) using RFC 1006, and any mapping of COTS onto X.25 (usually X.25(80)) where X.25 does not provide CONS. It is not appropriate where CONS or CLNS provide the transport service. For OSI over CLNS on the Internet, the guidelines of RFC 1237 apply.
sections.eli5: Some programs speak the OSI language but travel over other roads, like TCP/IP. This note gives them a way to write down where to go on those roads.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The RFC lists lower layers on which OSI applications run: international X.25 routed on X.121 addresses, large private X.25 networks such as Janet, isolated CONS and CLNS networks, a CLNP pilot, isolated TCP/IP LANs using RFC 1006, and the DARPA/NSF Internet using RFC 1006. These systems normally need transport bridging or application relaying, which causes problems and is not always possible.

The intended OSI solution is a single global network service where addresses imply nothing about routing. That only works in a pure OSI environment, so it does not solve this problem.
sections.eli5: In a perfect world every computer would use one kind of address. In the real world there are many roads, so a translation trick is needed.

sections.title: General Approach
sections.content:
Connecting to a remote Application Entity has four steps: look up the entity in the Directory to get a Presentation Address, extract each Network Address and decide whether and how it can be used, order the addresses by preference, and try to connect.

This note deals with the second step and probably affects the third. No directory service exists for step 2, so the approach is interim and must be algorithmic: all the addressing information needed for the network must be extracted from the network address itself.
sections.eli5: To call a friend you look up their number, check which phone can reach it, pick the best one and dial. This RFC helps with the checking part.

sections.title: X.121 Network Addresses
sections.content:
For end systems using the Connection Oriented Network Service with access to the international X.25 service, the RFC recommends the X.121 form of NSAP address relative to the access point. This lets routing across the public data networks use the X.121 addresses. Allocation of the Domain Specific Part (DSP) is a private issue.

If an X.121 address is interpreted, it provides a route by defining a subnetwork point of attachment on the international X.25 network; better routes may exist by private means. If the DSP is absent, the address implies mapping of Transport onto X.25(80).
sections.eli5: If a computer is already on the worldwide X.25 phone-style network, its own phone-style number can be used as its address.

sections.title: The New Address Format
sections.content:
The new format covers cases the X.121 form does not handle. Its requirements include that lower-layer information must come from the address, addresses must be globally unique, confusion with real CONS or CLNS addresses should be unlikely, and the network and its addressing must be deducible from the address.

The Initial Domain Part uses the Telex address type because it gives the largest DSP and is unlikely to be used for real network addresses. The DSP uses a decimal abstract encoding: a 2-digit prefix, then a network-specific part. The prefix plus the initial domain part identifies a subnetwork. The network-specific part should be under 20 digits for any initial domain format, and can be up to 27 for the Telex format.
sections.eli5: The address starts with a code that says which kind of network this is, then the rest of the number holds the details for that network.

sections.title: X.25(80) and TCP/IP Layouts
sections.content:
For X.25(80), the network-specific part starts with a 1-digit type: 0 for DTE only, 1 for DTE plus Protocol ID (PID), 2 for DTE plus CUDF, with 3 to 9 reserved. A PID/CUDF length follows, then the PID/CUDF with each octet written as three decimal digits, then the DTE number until the end of the address.

For TCP/IP with RFC 1006, the network-specific part is 20 digits: 12 digits of IP address, an optional 5-digit port (up to 65535, defaulting as in RFC 1006), and an optional 5-digit transport set, a 16-bit flag word where 1 is TCP and 2 is UDP. No bits set means the default, TCP. For example, 10.0.0.6 port 9 over UDP is encoded as 010 000 000 006, 00009, 00002.
sections.eli5: For a TCP/IP computer the long number is simply its IP address, port and kind of delivery, each padded with zeros to a fixed length.

sections.title: Allocated Prefixes
sections.content:
Appendix A allocates three well known networks under the supposed Telex number 00728722, used in pilot operations: International X.25 (prefix 01), Janet (prefix 02) and the DARPA/NSF Internet (prefix 03). IXI is listed with prefix 06. The international X.25 value is used only where a CUDF or PID is needed; otherwise an X.121 address with no DSP is used.

The values are in widespread use and must stay stable. UCL commits not to reassign the allocated space, and the DARPA/NSF Internet space (prefix 03) is delegated to the IANA. The RFC also says encoding for protocols is described in ISO 8348 Addendum 2, and that it has no security discussion.
sections.eli5: Each network gets a short code number, like area codes, and the people in charge promise not to change them.
